blocks.caption: Osmoregulation in three habitats
rows: the animal is hypertonic: water enters by osmosis (especially through the gills) and salts such as Na+ and Cl- diffuse out
produces large volumes of dilute urine; actively transports salts back in; rarely drinks
most marine animals are hypotonic: water leaves through gills and skin, and salts diffuse in and come with swallowed sea water
drinks sea water; makes small amounts of concentrated urine; chloride cells in the gills pump salts out using ATP; kidneys remove salts; some have rectal salt glands
water is lost by evaporation from breathing surfaces and skin and in wastes

waterproof coverings (chitin and wax in insects, keratin scales in reptiles, keratinized skin and oil glands in birds and mammals); water-saving kidneys; urea or uric acid instead of ammonia; behaviour such as staying underground by day

blocks.alt: Two fish; blue arrows show water, red arrows salts. (a) Freshwater fish: water and salts enter the mouth with food, salts are actively transported in at the gills, water enters through gills and other parts, and dilute urine leaves. (b) Marine fish: food and drinking water enter the mouth, salts are excreted through the gills, water is lost through gills and other parts, and concentrated urine leaves.
blocks.caption: Figure 13.4: Osmoregulation in (a) freshwater and (b) marine water (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 13.4).
blocks.long_description: Labels in (a): Food; Active transport of salts (red arrow into the gills); Entry of water through gills and other parts (four blue arrows into the body); Dilute urine (a long blue and a short red arrow at the vent). Labels in (b): Food & drinking water; Excretion of salts through gills (red arrow out of the gills); Water loss through gills and other parts (three blue arrows out of the body); Concentrated urine (a short blue and a long red arrow). The key shows a blue arrow for movement of water and a red arrow for movement of salts.

blocks.text: Many desert animals stay underground in the heat of the day and come out at night when the air is cooler and more humid, feeding on carbohydrate-rich seeds. The kangaroo rat can survive entirely on metabolic water, produced as a by-product of cellular respiration.

Some invertebrates such as tardigrades (water bears) survive losing almost all their body water by entering a dormant state called anhydrobiosis, and return to active life years later when water returns.
